text: Piccarda Is Dragged from the Convent: When Violence Changes a Person's Actions, How Far Can She Be Expected to Resist?
At first, Dante thinks he is seeing reflections.
Faces appear in a brightness as clear as moonlight.
As faint as images behind transparent glass.
Or faces reflected in shallow water, their outlines scarcely distinguishable from the background.
He turns his head to see whose images these really are.
There is nothing behind him.
Beatrice smiles.
What Dante sees are not shadows.
They are souls who have been saved.
One woman asks him to look closely and recognize her.
Her name is Piccarda.
Piccarda says she once entered the order of Saint Clare.
In youth, she left worldly life, put on the habit, and promised to follow that path until death.
Later, people more accustomed to evil than to good violently dragged her from the quiet convent.
Of the life that followed, she says only:
God knows.
Then she points to another luminous soul beside her.
That woman too had her habit forcibly removed and was taken back into the secular world.
Yet after her outward life changed, her inward attachment to the habit was never relinquished.
Piccarda does not call the violence her own choice.
Nor does she say that her inward direction changed with her departure.
But why does she appear in the sphere of the Moon?
She explains that she and the soul beside her neglected their vows and did not fulfill them completely.
Dante immediately encounters a difficulty.
If their good intention remained.
If their departure was caused by others' violence.
Why should there still seem to be a difference in their blessedness?
Can force exerted by others diminish the good due to a victim?
This is not a question imposed on Piccarda from outside the work.
The Paradiso itself lets Dante ask it.
Nor does Beatrice suppress it with “such is God's will.”
She acknowledges that it touches the apparent injustice of divine justice in human eyes.
Then she begins to distinguish violence from will.
Before going further, another point must be made clear.
Piccarda is not confined to a lower, worse heaven as punishment.
Beatrice explains that the true dwelling of all blessed souls is the Empyrean.
Their appearances now in the Moon, planets, and different heavenly spheres accommodate Dante's way of understanding through the senses, while making differences in degrees of blessedness visible.
Piccarda herself is completely happy.
Dante asks whether she wishes for a higher place, to see more and be closer to God.
She answers with a smile:
Love in Heaven makes everyone content with the order God has given.
If she desired another place, her wish would conflict with divine will.
God's will is their peace.
So this essay cannot portray her as waiting for vindication, punished for failing to resist successfully in life.
She is already in bliss.
The question is not whether Heaven has rejected her.
It is why the work still preserves differences in merit and steadfastness.
Beatrice first proposes the purest form of violence.
If the person subjected to force does not cooperate with its wielder at all, and the force merely twists her actions from outside, her will has not thereby consented.
She says the human will is not extinguished unless it also consents to some degree.
A truly steadfast will is like fire.
Even if force bends the flame elsewhere a thousand times, it still rises according to its nature.
Had Piccarda's and Constance's wills been as absolute and firm as a martyr's, they would have returned to the sanctuary along the path by which they were dragged away as soon as they had the chance.
But they did not.
So violence and will entered into a certain mixture in their later actions.
This is a very stringent account.
Beatrice then makes a finer distinction.
The absolute will did not consent to the wrong.
Inwardly, Piccarda did not recognize her forced departure from the order as the direction she truly wanted.
But another kind of will, operating under particular conditions, yields for fear of greater harm.
A person may do something she does not regard as good only because refusal would bring death, harm to loved ones, or some other worse outcome.
This does not mean that she wholeheartedly approves.
Nor can the action be called entirely unrelated to her.
So Piccarda speaks truly when she says that inwardly she never left the habit behind.
And Beatrice speaks truly when she says that Piccarda's actions under pressure still involved a measure of yielding.
The work refuses to divide will into only complete freedom or complete nonexistence.
This matters greatly.
Outwardly performing an action does not mean freely choosing it inwardly.
If a person is dragged out of a doorway and forced into another life, her body's later presence there cannot be called consent.
But saying no inwardly does not necessarily mean that none of her later actions are her own.
Under violence, a person may still judge.
Compare different dangers.
Choose what she considers the lesser evil in order to preserve life, protect others, or wait for an opportunity.
Acknowledging this limited agency does not transfer responsibility for the violence back to her.
It is, first, a refusal to portray an oppressed person as an object wholly without judgment.
Even when her choices are severely narrowed, she may still make certain responses within those confines.
The difficulty begins precisely here.
As soon as we acknowledge that a victim retains some agency, people can easily go on to say:
If she could still choose, why was she not firmer?
Why did she not escape?
Why did she not return later?
Why did she not choose death rather than submit?
Along this remnant of capacity, responsibility quickly flows back to the victim.
The people who used violence recede into the background.
As though what truly needed explaining were no longer who dragged her from the convent, but why she did not prove through death that she had never consented.
Paradiso Canto 4 uses martyrs as a reference for the most steadfast will.
Within the work's theological world, this is a standard of the highest virtue.
But the highest virtue and the minimum threshold of responsibility cannot easily be made the same thing.
A martyr would rather have the body burned than abandon the direction they have affirmed.
Such steadfastness can be praised.
But making it the minimum requirement for every victim of violence to prove innocence would be profoundly dangerous.
Only those who died could prove that they truly did not consent.
Survivors who yielded anywhere would be said to have given some willing cooperation.
Violence would thereby gain an advantage:
It forces people to choose between survival and fidelity.
Whichever side the victim chooses can be used to lessen the wielder's responsibility.
If she dies, she proves her fidelity.
If she lives, she is said not to have refused completely.
A supreme heroic choice should not be turned into a baseline ordinary people must meet or else bear responsibility for the consequences of violence.
This does not mean taking all judgment away from Piccarda.
If we said only:
She was carried off by force, so whatever she did afterward had nothing to do with her,
We would diminish her too.
A human life does not stop forever at the moment of victimization.
After violence changes her conditions, she may regain some choices, and may act within new relationships in ways for which she must answer herself.
Protecting a victim does not mean declaring that she is no longer an agent.
The real difficulty is preserving three things at once:
The original coercion must be named accurately.
Choices made under those conditions may still be hers.
That some part is hers must not make the primary responsibility for violence disappear.
Beatrice says they later had the capacity to return to the sanctuary.
If their will had been firm enough, they would have returned.
Within the work's theological judgment, this is a real premise.
Modern readers must nevertheless be careful.
The poem does not set out the practical ways out available to Piccarda after she was taken away.
She says only:
God knows what my life became afterward.
This sentence is not a blank sheet we are free to fill in.
After someone is forced out of one life, does the original door truly remain open?
Have family, marriage, reputation, surveillance, economic dependence, and threats to relatives already changed the conditions?
The poem does not tell us.
We cannot simply say that she needed only to turn around and return at no cost.
Nor can we declare the opposite, that she had absolutely no possibility at all.
The text's silence should remain silence.
“She did not go back later” cannot by itself automatically prove “she consented at the outset.”
Violence changes more than an action at one moment.
It changes the world of choices available afterward.
Someone forced into a new life may acquire new responsibilities, dependencies, and dangers.
The old identity may no longer be simply recoverable.
This does not mean that every later decision belongs to the perpetrator.
It means only that in judging why she did not return, we cannot pretend the initial violence did not change the route.
If someone is first pushed off a path, then asked why she did not walk straight back, the questioner must at least acknowledge:
The distance back was created by violence.
Piccarda's own account is very brief.
She does not accuse those who dragged her away at length.
Does not describe her later life.
Nor ask Dante for earthly compensation.
She is already in a peace fully consonant with divine will.
That peace cannot be understood to mean:
The original violence was therefore not really a problem.
A victim's later peace does not retrospectively make the act of harm right.
Nor does a person's ability to incorporate harm into a larger understanding of life give the one who harmed her permission.
Piccarda's happiness belongs to her present relationship with God.
Not to the defense of those who once used violence against her.
Nor does she ask for a higher heavenly sphere.
This often troubles modern readers.
If merit differs, why does she not feel an injustice?
Piccarda answers that love in Heaven produces no sense of lack through comparison.
Everyone's will accords with the whole order.
Viewed solely through earthly competition, her contentment would look like having been persuaded to accept a lower place.
But the work explicitly does not portray it this way.
She is not suppressing discontent.
Her happiness is real and complete.
So questioning Canto 4's severe theory of will cannot be accomplished by inventing a resentment Piccarda has not expressed.
We can examine the standard.
We cannot tell someone who has declared herself at peace that she is not really at peace.
What can truly be questioned is:
How can a system of judgment acknowledge violence, will, and limited choice at once, without allowing any one to swallow the other two?
Speaking only of violence leaves the person no place to act.
Speaking only of will makes coercion disappear.
Speaking only of the outcome mistakes what the body finally did for full inward consent.
Speaking only of inwardness, in turn, would mean the person need no longer answer for any outward action.
Beatrice's “absolute will” and “conditional will” are an attempt to avoid this dichotomy.
She acknowledges that a person may disapprove inwardly yet yield to avoid worse consequences.
The question is how we use this distinction.
To understand narrowed choices more precisely.
Or to search every concession for a share of blame to assign to the victim.
A fair judgment should at least begin by asking what the violent person did.
Who created the threat.
Who restricted the ways out.
What refusal would bring.
What the victim knew at the time.
Who else would share the consequences of her choice.
Whether there was an alternative that looks feasible not merely in hindsight.
Only then can we consider how far the actions still available are her own.
If all those questions are skipped, and we ask only:
Why did you not hold firm like a martyr?
What is called preserving agency becomes a subtler form of blame.
Not everyone who can still move at all has the capacity freely to change the entire situation.
Capacity is not merely present or absent.
Nor does a theoretically existing way out necessarily mean one can take it in practice.
Conversely, if someone under oppression truly regains a safe way out later, she may still need to answer for her choices.
Violence is not a certificate permanently canceling every responsibility.
Having once been coerced does not automatically absolve a person of later harm to others under entirely different conditions.
Having lost a direction does not mean there can never be a chance to affirm it anew.
This is precisely why a place for action must be preserved.
It does more than entitle others to question her.
It also entitles the victim to say:
This later part is a decision I made anew.
Not something the violent person forever decides for me.
Attributing her entire subsequent life to the original coercion would instead give the coercer permanent ownership of her time.
Piccarda's story does not provide such a complete later life.
In the sphere of the Moon, it lets her say only:
I once chose the order.
I was taken away by force.
In my heart, the habit was never laid aside.
My vows were not completely fulfilled.
I am now entirely at peace.
There is tension among these sentences.
The Paradiso does not dissolve it into “she is guilty” or “she bears no responsibility.”
Dante's question remains.
Beatrice answers with a severe and complex theory of will.
Readers today need not pretend that it contains no difficulties.
Nor must they call the work nothing but victim-blaming in order to identify those difficulties.
The text's real force lies in compelling us to face this:
Violence does not always destroy a person's will completely.
And not destroying it completely does not mean that the violence has been consented to.
When Piccarda finishes speaking, she begins to sing the Ave Maria.
As she sings, she vanishes from Dante's sight.
The poem says she is like a heavy object sinking into deep water.
It is a strange image.
She was as faint as a reflection on water.
Now, like something with weight, she recedes deeper into the light.
Her story is the same.
Very little is said.
Its weight does not thereby disappear.
We do not know her whole life after the violence.
We cannot supply a complete autobiography for her.
We know only that she was dragged from the path she had affirmed.
And that the work refuses to make her someone entirely without will because of it.
When violence changes a person's actions, how far can she be expected to resist?
The answer cannot simply be:
As long as any capacity remains, she should resist to the end.
Nor can it simply be:
Once there has been violence, every subsequent action has nothing to do with her.
What must be preserved is a narrow and difficult boundary:
A person under pressure may still act within limited conditions.
This leaves her a person, not an object moved by external force.
But her actions must be understood together with the narrowed options, the cost of refusal, and the later world violence has created.
The highest martyrdom can be praised.
It cannot become the minimum requirement for every survivor to prove that they did not consent.
Otherwise, violence changes more than her life.
It also gains the power to explain why she failed to destroy herself.

*Textual basis: Dante, Divine Comedy, Paradiso Cantos 3 and 4. In Canto 3, Dante initially mistakes the souls in the sphere of the Moon for reflections. Piccarda identifies herself and explains that those appearing here did not completely fulfill their vows, while explicitly stating that all the blessed have wills in harmony with divine order and are entirely at peace (Par. 3.10–90). She says that in youth she entered the order of Saint Clare, then was violently dragged from the “sweet convent” by people accustomed to wrongdoing; “God knows” her subsequent life. Constance too was forced to leave, but never laid aside the habit in her heart (approximately 3.97–120). In Canto 4, Dante asks why others' violence should affect merit if good intention remains. Beatrice first explains that all the souls actually dwell in the Empyrean, with their appearances in different spheres accommodating human understanding (approximately 4.28–63). She then distinguishes purely external violence, absolute will, and conditional will that yields for fear of greater harm, taking the martyr-like steadfastness of Lawrence and Mucius as the highest reference (approximately 4.64–117). This essay does not portray Piccarda as being punished on the Moon, nor directly transfer the work's standard of the highest virtue into the minimum threshold by which everyone under coercion must prove innocence.*
